abstract: |
  This report presents the 2025 assessment of the conservation status of Norwegian species and habitats 
  as mandated by Resolution 8 of the Bern Convention. The evaluation comprises 157 detailed assessments 
  covering 72 species and 6 habitat types across Norway's four bio-geographical regions. Statuses were 
  categorized on a four-grade scale as *Favourable*, *Unfavourable inadequate*, *Unfavourable bad*, or 
  *Unknown* based on parameters including range, population size or habitat area, habitat quality, and 
  future prospects.  
  
  The findings reveal that a significant number of the assessed features currently hold "Unfavourable" overall 
  conservation status. Primary ongoing pressures affecting these species and habitats include problematic 
  native species, infrastructure development, land conversion, and climate change. Correspondingly, top 
  conservation measures focus on preventing natural habitat conversion and adapting forest management practices.  
  
  While the report highlights notable conservation successes—such as a tenfold population increase in the 
  critically endangered Arctic fox due to targeted interventions like captive breeding and feeding—it also 
  underscores severe knowledge gaps. Optimal quantitative data is largely restricted to specific monitored 
  mammals and fish, whereas 18 species and habitat types currently suffer from highly fragmented or entirely 
  absent foundational distribution data.

```{r}
h_lkp <- function(x, tab) { # generic lookup (x: any vec; tab: a df or mat w cols 1/2 containing lkp keys/values)
  tab[[2]][match(as.character(x), as.character(tab[[1]]))]
  } 
h_cap1st <- function(x) x %>% #capitalise just the first letters of a chr vector (all subsequent letters kept)
  str_sub(1,1) %>% toupper %>% str_c(str_sub(x,2)) 
h_ensure_cols <- function(x, cols, typ="") { # make sure that columns _cols_ exist in _x_ 
  new_cols <- cols[!cols %in% names(x)]      # (create them with NAs (of the type of typ) if needed)
  ret <- typ %>% c(NA, .) %>% {.[1]} %>% 
    rep(length(new_cols)) %>% set_names(new_cols) %>% 
    as.list %>% bind_cols(x, .)
  ret <- if (nrow(x)!=0L) ret else slice(ret, -1)
  ret}
```

## Context and purpose

The Bern Convention, adopted in 1979, is an international treaty aimed at conserving wild plant and animal species and their natural habitats in several non-EU European and North-African countries. It legally binds its member countries to protect over 1,000 animal species and 500 plant species, focusing on species and habitats that require cross-border cooperation. A relatively new amendment (Resolution 8, 2012) extended the Bern Convention with a network of Emerald sites and the implementation of management, monitoring, and reporting measures for them. The Emerald Network is the Pan-European equivalent of the EU's Natura 2000 network, and this resolution provides the framework for how countries designate and manage these ecological sites. In Norway the Emerald sites largely (but not entirely) correspond to the other existing protected areas (see @fig-bgr-emerald). 

```{r}
#| label: fig-bgr-emerald
#| fig-cap: "The four EU biogeographical regions (BGR), and the Emerald Network in Norway"
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-align: "center"
#| echo: false
#| warning: false

knitr::include_graphics(here::here("img","bgr_emerald.png"))
```

According to *Resolution 8* (2012), every country must perform regular reporting about a selection of *species* and *habitat types*. As the Bern Convention has a Pan-European focus, it covers several species and habitat types that are threatened at the European level, even if they are doing relatively fine in Norway. Monitoring and reporting for such species can be considered as a vital contribution from Norway to their European-level protection. Similarly, the Resolution 8 reporting may miss some nationally/regionally endangered species and ha-bitat types if they are not under threat at the European level, which underlines why national and international monitoring and reporting must be sustained in parallel, maximising their sy-nergies.

The structure and content of the reporting, as well as its timing follows very closely the so-called “Article 17 reporting” of the EU Habitats Directive. Furthermore, both reporting processes have a *6-year cycle*, which means that for the Bern Convention countries the 2025 reporting is their second reporting altogether (the first, relatively limited reporting took place in 2019). The main purpose of the whole reporting is to assess the “*conservation status*” of the selected species and habitats in a semi-standardised way, based on the best available data and evidence.

The heart of the Resolution 8 reporting consists of a series of detailed assessments that address a number of pre-selected, species, habitat types and *biogeographic regions* (BGR, see @fig-bgr-emerald). For 2025 Norway received a “checklist” consisting of 74 *species* and 6 *habitat types*, which are often also called *features* collectively. Each of these features was pre-selected for *assessment* in one or more of the four EU biogeographic regions (BGR) that intersect the territory of the country.[^0] Eventually, the presence of three species was not confirmed by the experts,[^1] and the list of biogeographic regions also had to be updated for several species. This resulted in a final set 157 *full assessments* covering 71 *species* 6 *habitat types* across the four biogeographic regions of Norway (@tbl-fgrp-occ).[^2] The full list of the species and habitat types assessed and the main assessment conclusions is presented in Annexes 1 & 2.   

[^0]: In the context of the Bern Convention, assessing one feature (a species or a habitat type) in one region is counted as "one assessment".  
[^1]: Stag beetle (*Lucanus cervus*) was never observed in Norway, and two species, the beetle *Stephanopachys substriatus* and the orchid *Liparis loeselei* disappeared from Norway before the Bern Convention entered into force.  
[^2]: Pre-defined special cases (e.g. species/habitats with *marginal presence* (MAR) or uncertain occurrence (*scientific reserve*, SCR)) in the studied region. For these *occurrence categories* we did not provide a detailed assessment in this assessment period. 

```{r}
#| label: tbl-fgrp-occ
#| tbl-cap: "The number of *features* (i.e. species & habitat types: N~features~) and *assessments* (detailed expert evaluations for a feature in a biogeofraphic region: N~assessments~). Features (species, habitats) with insignificant, uncertain, or historical occurrences in a biogeographic region were recorded without a detailed assessment (MAR: Features near their natural range limits with insignificant abundance/area in the studied region; EXp: Species extinct before the Bern Convention entered into force (1982); SCR: Features with an uncertain occurrence in the studied region)."
#| warning: false

### an overview table
tmp1a <- select(dat2$spr, ftid, bgr, occ)  %>% 
  bind_rows(select(dat2$har, ftid, bgr, occ)) %>%
  mutate(fgrp= h_lkp(ftid, select(chklw, ftid, fgrp)) %>% fct(names(fgrps_en))) %>%
  group_by(fgrp, occ) %>% summarise(value= n()) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from="occ") %>%
  mutate(Na= PRE+replace_na(TAX, 0)) %>%
  select(Na, MAR, EXp, SCR) #drop "DEL" and sort the rest (## )+drop PRE & TAX too -- as reported under Na)
tmp1 <- select(dat2$spr, ftid, bgr, occ)  %>% 
  bind_rows(select(dat2$har, ftid, bgr, occ)) %>%
  mutate(fgrp= h_lkp(ftid, select(chklw, ftid, fgrp)) %>% fct(names(fgrps_en))) %>%
  group_by(fgrp) %>% summarise(Nf= length(unique(ftid))) %>%
  left_join(tmp1a, by="fgrp") %>%
  mutate(main= str_c(fgrps_en[as.character(fgrp)]," (",fgrp,")") %>% unname) %>%
  relocate(main) %>% select(-fgrp)
tmp2 <- tmp1 %>% summarise(main= "Total", across(-main, \(x) sum(x, na.rm=T)))
  
bind_rows(tmp1, tmp2) %>% gt() %>% 
  cols_label(main="Feature groups", Nf=md("N~features~"), Na=md("N~assessments~")) %>%
  tab_spanner(label="Special cases", columns=-c(main, Nf, Na)) %>%
  cols_align("center") %>% cols_align("left", columns= main) %>%
  sub_missing() %>%
  tab_style(style = cell_text(weight= "bold"), locations = cells_column_labels()) %>%
  tab_style(style = cell_text(v_align= "top"), locations = cells_body()) %>%
  tab_options(table.width = pct(100), data_row.padding = px(3))

```


## Conservation status of species and habitat types 

We start with presenting an overview of the conclusions of the assessments. Each assessment has an overall conclusion, which is based on four "parameters", each of which has its own conclusions. The conclusions for the individual parameters rely on quantitative and qualitative data collected by taxonomic experts following detailed guidelines provided by the Bern Secretariat. The four assessment parameters for species include its *distribution range* (Ran), *population size* (Pop), the quality and quantity of the *available habitat* for the species (H4s), and its *future prospects* (Fpr) based on the balance of pressures and conservation measures. All conclusions are evaluated in a simple "traffic light system" using one of the following four *conservation status* categories: 

*  **FV**: Favourable (green), 
*  **U1**: Unfavourable - inadequate (amber), 
*  **U2**: Unfavourable - bad (red),
*  **XX**: Unknown (grey).

### Species assessments

@tbl-conclusions-sp-fgrp provides an overview of the overall conclusions across the major species groups, whereas @tbl-conclusions-sp-para shows the distribution of the partial conclusions for the individual parameters across all the species.

## Changes and trends

The assessment protocol offers several ways to describe past, present and future trends in the conservation status of the studied species and habitats. This includes the assessment of the *short-term* and *long-term* trends by the experts participating in the 2025 assessment, as well as a direct comparisons of the consecutive assessments (e.g comparing the conservation status of the same species & habitats assessed in 2019 and 2025). In the context of the Bern Convention *short-term trends* always refer to the past 12 years (i.e. 2013-2024 in this case), whereas *long term trends* are referring to the 24 year period before the assessment date (i.e. 2001-2024). In addition, the parameter *future prospects* discussed in the previous section also addresses trends, synthesizing expectations for changes in the other three parameters during the forthcoming 12 years (i.e. 2025-2036). 

In the next few sections we provide an overview of the main current and past trends relying on the different elements of the Bern assessment protocol.    

### Short term trends

Short term trends are first assessed individually for the different state parameters (range, population size, and habitat availability for species, and range, area, and structure/function for habitat types), and then the directions of these elementary trends are aggregated into an *overall trend qualifier*, which is the second flagship output of Bern Convention assessments, providing critical insights for the interpretation of the *overall conservation status*. In @fig-trend-qualifiers we provide an overview of these trend qualifiers for the different groups of features.     

:::{#fig-trend-qualifiers layout="[[1, 1],[8,7,3,7,3]]"}
```{r}
#| label: qualifiers_1a
#| warning: false
#| echo: false

lov <- stcodes %>% filter(id=="rd_ConclusionsTrend") %>% select(sc,sl) %>% deframe

### overall trend qualifiers per species groups
tmp1 <- dat2$spr %>%
  select(Codes= S_11_6_conclusion_overall_trend) %>% 
  bind_rows(dat2$har %>% select(Codes= H_10_6_conclusion_overall_trend)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(Codes)) %>%
  mutate(Codes=Codes %>% str_sub(1,1) %>% fct(names(lov))) %>%
  group_by(Codes) %>% summarise(n=n()) 

# the overall trend qualifiers (pie) 
tmp1 %>% 
  {ggplot(.) + geom_bar(aes(x="", y=n, fill=Codes), stat="identity", width=1, color="white") +
  scale_fill_manual(name="Trend direction", labels=lov, 
                    values= c(I="yellowgreen",S="gold2",D="darkorange",U="ivory3")) +
  coord_polar(theta="y", direction=-1) + 
  theme_void(base_size= 16)}

```

```{r}
#| label: qualifiers_1b
#| warning: false
#| echo: false

tmp2 <- dat2$spr %>%
  mutate(fgrp= h_lkp(ftid, select(chklw, ftid, fgrp)) %>% fct(names(fgrps_en))) %>%
  select(fgrp, Codes= S_11_6_conclusion_overall_trend) %>% 
  bind_rows(dat2$har %>% mutate(fgrp=fct("ht",names(fgrps_en))) %>% select(fgrp, Codes= H_10_6_conclusion_overall_trend)) %>%
  mutate(Codes=Codes %>% str_sub(1,1) %>% fct(names(lov))) %>%
```

### Changes in conservation status since 2019

The 2019 reporting period was the first reporting period for Norway under Resolution 8 of the Bern Convention. This reporting period was considered to be a pilot exercise by the Bern Convention Secretariat, so only very few species and habitat types were selected for reporting. @tbl-changes-19 provides an overview of the changes in the overall assessment conclusions for the overlapping species.

```{r}
#| echo: false
```

If the overall conservation status of a species/habitat changed since 2019 then the experts were were requested to assess the main reasons for the change. They could select more then one reason from a list that included *genuine change*, changes in *data* or *methods*. The results are summarised in @tbl-change-reasons-19.

```{r}

  select(ftid, bgr, rl_navn, fgrp, data= S_11_7_a_conclusions_overall_assesment_change) 
tmp2 <- dat2$har %>%
  mutate(fgrp= h_lkp(ftid, select(chklw, ftid, fgrp)) %>% fct(names(fgrps_en))) %>%
  mutate(rl_navn= h_lkp(ftid, select(chklw, ftid, rl_navn))) %>%

tmp2 %>% gt() %>%
```

## Background factors 

A major element of the Bern Convention (Resolution 8) reporting protocol is the assessment of *pressures* (i.e. threats) and *conservation measures* affecting the status and trends of the selected species and habitat types. These factors have a key role in the assessment of the *future prospects* parameter, but and they can also provide relevant information by  themselves, e.g. for effective conservation planning. The assessment protocol offers a long list of predefined types of pressures and conservation measures, and the experts could choose from these lists, assigning an ordered list of *pressures* and *measures* to each species and habitat type. 
<!-- In addition, the experts also characterised each pressure and measure from the perspective of several further properties, specifying e.g. if a pressure is an ongoing or only an expected future threat, and approximately what portion of the population is affected by it.  -->

### Key pressures

Beyond just listing the relevant pressures the experts also had to characterise them from three different perspectives: its timing (past, ongoing or expected future pressure), extent (the share of the population/area it affects), and influence (the degree of impact on the affected population/area). @tbl-press-list presents an overview of the pressures that were most commonly listed as "ongoing" threats across all species and habitat types.

```{r}
#| tbl-cap: "The 20 most most commmon active (ongoing) pressures identified during the assessments (N: number of assessments where the given pressure was identified; ma: mammals, fa= fishes & amphibians, im= insects and molluscs, vp: vascular plants, mo: mosses, ht: habitat types)"
#| warning: false
#| echo: false

  select(ftid, fgrp, rl_navn, bgr, s1=S_8_1_a_pressure_code, s2=S_8_1_b_timing) #%>%

  select(ftid, fgrp, rl_navn, bgr, s1=H_7_1_a_pressure_code, s2=H_7_1_b_timing) %>%  
  bind_rows(tmp1a)
```

### Main conservation measures

Similarly to the pressures, the experts also identified the most important conservation measures for each feature in each biogeographic region. This included all "ongoing" (actively implemented) conservation measures, as well as any clearly useful, but not yet implemented measures. In addition, for each already implemented measure the experts also documented if the measures were implemented only within the Emerald sites, or also beyond them. @tbl-meas-list presents an overview of the most frequently mentioned conservation measures.

### Role of the Emerald Network

Protected areas, and in particular the Emerald Network is assumed to provide substantial support for endangered species and habitats. Several parts of the Bern assessment explore the influence of the Emerald Network, thus providing useful feedback for conservation management. In @tbl-eme-trends we compare *within Emerald* short-term trends of several parameters with the general trends of the same parameters within the entire biogeographic region. This comparison is only sensitive to the direction of the trend, so significant differences between slight and drastic declines (or improvements) can still be marked as "same within/beyond Emerald" in @tbl-eme-trends.      


```{r}
#| label: tbl-eme-trends
#| tbl-cap: "Comparison of short term trends in several parameters within the Emerald network and outside of it." 
#| warning: false
#| echo: false

lov <-  c(better= "Better *within* Emerald", same= "Same trend within/beyond", 
          worse=  "Better *beyond* Emerald", unk=  "Unknown (at least partly)") 

# para <- list(Pop=c("A4a","A4c"), H4s=c("C3a","C3b"), Are= c("A2a","A2c"), SnF=c("C3a","C3b"))
para <- list(Pop=c("S_6_10","S_12_6"), H4s=c("S_7_4","S_12_8"), Are= c("H_5_7","H_11_4"), SnF=c("H_6_4","H_11_6")) %>%
  map(\(y) map_chr(y, \(x) str_subset(c(names(dat2$spr),names(dat2$har)), str_c("^",x))[1]))
tmp <-  c(Pop="spr", H4s="spr", Are="har", SnF="har")

tmp2 <- para %>%
  imap(\(x,i) dat2[[tmp[i]]] %>% mutate(c_reg= !!rlang::sym(x[1]), c_eme= !!rlang::sym(x[2]))) %>%
  map( \(x)   x %>% filter(!is.na(c_reg)) %>% filter(c_reg!="")) %>%
  map( \(x)   x %>% mutate(rl_navn= h_lkp(ftid, select(chklw, ftid, rl_navn)))) %>%
  map( \(x)   x %>% mutate(c_eme=str_sub(c_eme,1,1), c_reg=str_sub(c_reg,1,1))) %>%
  imap(\(x,i) x %>% mutate(para=i, cc= str_c(c_eme, c_reg))) %>%
  map( \(x)   x %>% group_by(para, cc) %>% summarise(N=n(), spp= list(sort(unique(rl_navn))), .groups="drop")) %>%
  list_rbind %>%
  # mutate(cc= if_else(str_detect(cc, "U"), NA, cc)) %>%
  mutate(cc2= case_match(cc, c("SD","ID","IS") ~ "better",
                             c("DD","SS","II") ~ "same",
                             c("DS","DI","SI") ~ "worse")) %>%
  mutate(cc2= replace_na(cc2, "unk") %>% fct(names(lov))) %>%
  group_by(para, cc2) %>% summarise(N=sum(N), spp=list(sort(unique(list_c(spp)))), .groups="drop") %>%
  arrange(cc2)
tmp2b <- tmp2 %>%
  select(-spp) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from= para, values_from= N) %>% 
  relocate(!!!c("cc2", names(para0_en[names(tmp)]))) %>%
  mutate(cc2= lov[cc2])

tmp2b %>% gt() %>% 
  cols_label(.list= c(cc2="Trends within/beyond Emerald", para0_en[names(tmp)])) %>%
  cols_align("center") %>% cols_align("left", columns= cc2) %>%
  sub_missing() %>%
  fmt_markdown(columns= cc2) %>% #!!!
  tab_style(style = cell_text(weight = "bold"), locations = cells_column_labels()) %>%
  tab_options(table.width = pct(100), data_row.padding = px(3))

```

```{r}
#| label: txt-eme-trends-diag
#| warning: false
#| echo: true

# A quick temporary overview of the most interesting cases of the table above:
tmp2 %>% 
  filter(para %in% c("Pop", "H4s"), cc2 %in% c("better", "worse")) %>%
  mutate(species=map_chr(spp, \(x) str_c(x, collapse=", "))) %>%
  select(para, cc2, species) %>%
  print

```


In addition we can also compare the implementation of the conservation measures within and beyond the Emerald Network based on the answers of the experts. @tbl-eme-meas offers such a comparison. 

```{r}
#| label: tbl-eme-meas
#| tbl-cap: "The location of the most frequently implemented conservation measures: predominantly within Emerald sites (N~in~), mostly outside of the Emerald Network (N~out~), or both within and beyond Emerald (N~i.o~)"
#| warning: false
#| echo: false

tmp0 <- c(i="inside", io="both", o="outside")
tmp1.meas %>%
  filter(s4=="T") %>%  # "T" means taken
  group_by(s1) %>% summarise(N=n(), tmp=list(map(tmp0, \(x) sum(s2==x)))) %>% 
  mutate(tmp= map(tmp, as_tibble)) %>% unnest(tmp) %>% 
  arrange(desc(N)) %>%
  mutate(label= h_lkp(s1, pmcodes)) %>%
  relocate(s1, label) %>% slice(1:10) %>% 
  # select(-N) %>%
  gt() %>%
  sub_missing() %>%
  cols_label(s1="Code", label="Conservation measure name", N=md("N~tot~"), 
             i=md("N~in~"), io=md("N~i.o~"), o=md("N~out~")) %>%
  cols_align("center") %>% cols_align("left", columns= label) %>%
  # cols_width(label ~ pct(80)) %>%
  tab_style(style = cell_text(weight= "bold"), locations = cells_column_labels()) %>%
  tab_style(style = cell_text(v_align= "top"), locations = cells_body()) %>%
  tab_options(table.width = pct(100), data_row.padding = px(3))

```


## Bevaring av fjellreven en suksess – tidobling av bestanden

Fjellreven har lenge vært kritisk truet i Norge. Arten ble fredet allerede i 1930, men fortsatte å gå tilbake. Bestanden var trolig allerede da for liten til å respondere positivt på vern, samtidig ble det observert store endring i smågnagerdynamikken og økt forekomst av rødrev på tundraen, som kan ha påvirket fjellreven negativt. 
Rundt 2000 antok man at bestanden bare talte 40-60 voksne individer i Norge, Sverige og Finland til sammen. Arten var da svært nær å bli utryddet. Med bakgrunn i den første handlingsplanen for arten, kom tiltakene i Norge i gang fra 2005. Avlsprogrammet for fjellrev ble da etablert på fjellet og har per nå satt ut over 500 fjellrev. I tillegg til å reetablere fem utdødde norske delbestander har utsatte fjellrever bidratt til å styrke mange av de gjenværende delbestandene i Fennoskandia og også medført reetablering i Finland. Det ble da også satt i gang støttefôring, og det er per nå mer enn 150 fôrautomater i drift gjennom hele året i så godt som hele utbredelsen. Det tredje tiltaket, systematisk uttak av rødrev, gjøres bare i den nordligste delen av utbredelsen, og ellers bare der rødreven er i direkte konkurranse med fjellreven. Tiltakene har resultert i en tidobling av bestanden, nå beregnet til å være over 300 voksne fjellrev i Norge. Som følge av det ble fjellreven listet til sterkt truet i 2021 (@fig-fjellrev-bestand). 

I Norge finnes fjellreven bare i det alpine og arktiske biomet, hvorav 85-90% i det alpine tundrabiomet. Bare 10-15% av bestanden finnes utenfor Emerald nettverket. Beskyttelsen verneområdene er gitt, blant annet gjennom strenge restriksjoner på utbygging av infrastruktur, anlegg og bygninger har trolig bidratt sterkt til at det fortsatt er bæreevne for fjellrev i disse områdene. Restriksjoner på utbygging i store deler av tundrabiomet gjør at områdene beholder sin naturlige marginalitet som høyfjellsartene er særdeles godt tilpasset. Økt menneskelig aktivitet fører alltid med seg høyere tetthet av generalistarter, blant annet rødrev,  som kan fortrenge fjellreven om den opptrer i høye tettheter.   

```{r}
#| label: fig-fjellrev-bestand
#| fig-cap: "Estimert bestandsstørrelse (med 95 % konfidensintervaller) for fjellrev i Norge i perioden 2008–2025, basert på en lukket fangst-gjenfangst modell bygget på innsamlet DNA-materiale i den samme perioden. Rød linje viser glidende gjennomsnitt over 3-årsperioder. Merk at gjennomsnittses-timatene er sentrert, dvs. estimatet for 2023–2025 vises som estimat på 2024 i figuren. (Fra Jackson mfl. 2025)"
#| out-width: "90%"
#| fig-align: "center"
#| echo: false
#| warning: false

knitr::include_graphics(here::here("img","fjellrev_bestand.png"))
```

Vern av leveområdene, omfang og ikke minst varigheten av tiltakene har vært avgjørende for suksessen av bevaringsarbeidet. Tross suksessen og tidoblingen, er fjellrevbestanden fortsatt langt fra å være levedyktig, blant annet på grunn av lav konnektivitet og utfordringer med innavl. Forskerne anslår at tiltakene må vedvare med samme intensitet 10-15 år til, før man kan begynne å trappe ned arbeidet. 
Bevaringsarbeidet er finansiert av Miljødirektoratet, tidvis med bidrag fra InterReg. Det praktiske arbeidet gjøres i hovedsak av Statens naturoppsyn, NINA har ansvar for den faglige koordineringen av tiltakene og overvåking av bestanden, samt drift av avlsprogrammet (@fig-fjellrev-photo).

## Data availability

Resolution 8 Assessments for the Bern Convention rely on several types of data. The most important data types include detailed *spatial data* characterising the actual distribution of the studied species and habitat types, reliable *quantitative data* about the actual population size (species) or area extent (habitats), and a reliable quantitative *reference level* for this population/area. While spatial distribution and quantitative population/extent can change rapidly, and thus demand careful monitoring, the reference levels only need to established once (e.g. using population viability modelling techniques), and then they can be reused in subsequent reporting cycles. These data types are also necessary for proper conservation planning and management at the national level. In @tbl-data-avail we provide an overview of the availability of these key data types.[^meth] 

[^meth]: For the main quantitative fields the experts had to characterise the methodology and their level of certainty (high/medium/low "quality of information"). Here we started out from these responses.  

```{r}
#| label: tbl-data-avail
#| tbl-cap: "The studied species and habitats grouped according to data availability" 
#| warning: false
#| echo: false

lkp_met1 <- c(estimatePartial="L", completeSurvey="M") 
lkp_met2 <- c(absentData="L", estimateExpert="L", estimatePartial="M", completeSurvey="H") 

lov <-  c(MH1= "Reliable quantitative data with ref.levels",
          MH0= "Reliable quantitative data without ref.levels",
          MM1= "Partial/expert data with ref.levels",
          MM0= "Partial/expert data without ref.levels",
          ML0= "Spat. distribution data & qualitative estimates",
          LL0= "No or very fragmented data")

tmp1a <- dat2$sp %>% select(ftid, spdm= S_2_4_distribution_method) %>%
  bind_rows(dat2$ha %>% select(ftid, spdm= H_2_3_distribution_method)) %>%
  mutate(spdm= lkp_met1[spdm] %>% replace_na("L") %>% unname)

tmp1b <- dat2$spr %>% select(ftid, bgr, cvm= S_6_7_population_size_method) %>%
  bind_rows(dat2$har %>% select(ftid, bgr, cvm= H_5_4_area_method)) %>%
  mutate(cvm= lkp_met2[cvm] %>% replace_na("L") %>% unname %>% fct(c("L","M","H")) %>% ordered) %>%
  group_by(ftid) %>% summarise(cvm=max(cvm))

tmp1c <- dat2$spr %>% select(ftid, bgr, frvm= S_6_18_c_favourable_reference_population_unknown) %>%
  bind_rows(dat2$har %>% select(ftid, bgr, frvm= H_5_15_c_favourable_reference_area_unknown)) %>%
  mutate(frvm= if_else(frvm=="Yes","0","1") %>% replace_na("0")) %>% 
  # mutate(frvm2= frvm2 %>% replace_na("L") %>% fct(names(lov2_met)) %>% ordered) %>%
  group_by(ftid) %>% summarise(frvm=max(frvm))

tmp1 <- tmp1a %>%
  full_join(tmp1b) %>% full_join(tmp1c) %>%
  mutate(cvm= if_else(spdm=="L", "L", cvm)) %>% #if there is ~no spatial data then pop/area cannot be properly estimated either
  mutate(frvm= if_else(cvm=="L", "0", frvm)) %>% #if there is ~no data on pop/area then the frv should not be taken seriously
  mutate(ccc= str_c(spdm, cvm, frvm) %>% fct(names(lov))) %>%
  mutate(fgrp= h_lkp(ftid, select(chklw, ftid, fgrp)) %>% fct(names(fgrps_en))) %>%
  mutate(rl_navn= h_lkp(ftid, select(chklw, ftid, rl_navn))) %>%
  group_by(ccc) %>% summarise(N=n(), feat= str_c(rl_navn, collapse=", ") %>% h_cap1st) %>%
  arrange(ccc)

tmp1 %>% 
  mutate(ccc= lov[ccc]) %>%
  gt() %>% 
  cols_label(ccc= "Data availability", feat= "Features (species, habitat types)") %>%
  cols_align("left") %>%
  sub_missing() %>%
  tab_style(style = cell_text(weight= "bold"), locations = cells_column_labels()) %>%
  tab_style(style = cell_text(v_align= "top"), locations = cells_body()) %>%
  tab_options(table.width = pct(100), data_row.padding = px(3))

```

For most of the species, data availability is a major limitation for Bern Convention assessments. There are relatively few species with «optimal» data availability, including mainly charismatic and economically important mammal and fish species with dedicated monitoring programmes. For most of the Bern species and habitat types there are some spatial distribution data available (covering more than 75% of the presumable distribution of the species), but there are no representative monitoring programmes. For 18 species and habitat types, however, even their basic spatial distribution is poorly known. For habitat types this is often also related to the differences between the Norwegian national habitat typologies (e.g. NiN 2.3 or 3.0) and the EUNIS typology used by the Bern Convention.
